extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy, literature, and humour studies
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and comparing historical philosophical criteria for humour (notably Hobbesian superiority and eighteenth-century incongruity accounts), and social norms for appropriate wit. Focuses on cognitive, moral and social standards used by theorists to characterize, evaluate or prescribe forms of laughter and wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superiority theory (Hobbes)
rubrics_metrics.description: We experience superiority when we laugh; laughter is a sudden glory or triumph in ourselves from comparison with others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes framed laughter as arising from a feeling of superiority and used it to support a wider political argument: that laughter indicates selfish motives and undermines social relations. Examples/implications: a society filled with laughter would be a place of mockery where each tries to outdo everyone else. Anti-pattern: treating laughter as purely innocent pleasure ignores its social and political dangers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter as socially disruptive / indicator of anti-social motives
rubrics_metrics.description: The apparently innocent joy of laughter is not so innocent; it indicates an unpleasant feeling that strikes at social relations and can threaten social order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes argued that unchecked passions (including laughter rooted in superiority) would threaten social order, justifying external controls (state, religion). Use this criterion when assessing the social function or consequences of humour: does it promote mockery, rivalry, or social destabilization? Historical context: Hobbes wrote amid violent times and used the argument to justify authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phenomenological counter-claim: lack of felt superiority (Hutcheson and others)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics report that in ordinary laughter (e.g., cheerful conversation among friends) people seldom feel a sense of superiority; the supposed pleasure from others' misfortunes is often not consciously experienced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hutcheson: 'the apparent feeling of superiority ... seldom arises in our minds in the hurry of a cheerful conversation.' Use this as an empirical/experiential test of Hobbes: introspective reports challenge the universality of superiority as the cause of laughter. Anti-pattern: taking Hobbes's introspective claim at face value without accounting for self-report limits or self-deception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-deception as explanation for denial of superiority
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when people deny feeling superiority, this may reflect self-deception: we call selfish motives by noble names and conceal our desires from ourselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes lacked a full psychology of self-deception, but his claim implies that denial of superiority in introspection does not necessarily refute the theory. Use caution when evaluating theories purely on self-report; later psychological developments (e.g., Freudian thought) provide tools for analysing concealed motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity theory (basic formulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter arises from the perception of incongruity — the conjunction of objects or circumstances not usually combined; connecting different ideas suddenly provokes comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Developed as reaction to Hobbes: emphasises cognitive mechanisms (perception, judgement, surprise) rather than emotional superiority. Quotations: Locke (assemblage of ideas...), Kames ('A junction of things by distant and fanciful relations, which surprise because they are unexpected'), Akenside (ridicule linked to perception of incongruous form). Use this criterion to evaluate humour that depends on unexpected connections, metaphorical leaps, or surprising analogies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of surprise and unexpectedness in wit
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit operates by drawing together ideas listeners do not expect; the surprise in connecting dissimilar items is central to comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stewart and others stress surprise as essential. Locke: wit 'brings together ideas ... thereby to make up pleasant pictures'. When assessing a witty remark, check whether it produces unexpected congruity and cognitive surprise rather than merely reiterating common associations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit versus judgement (Locke's distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit is the quick assemblage of ideas producing a fanciful impression; judgement is careful discrimination of similarity and difference — wit is superficially pleasing but lacks the depth of slow, careful judgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to evaluate types of humour: witty cleverness (speed, memory, fanciful resemblance) may be praised for liveliness but critiqued for superficiality. Example/illustration: Samuel Johnson's quip comparing a poem to a cucumber — clever but not deep. Anti-pattern: valuing wit solely for cleverness while ignoring substantive judgement or depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity as cognitive (not emotional) mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: The incongruity theory posits a purely intellectual response — a 'modification of thought activity' — rather than an emotional feeling like Hobbes's superiority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: James Sully and others describe incongruity as 'bloodless': stimuli are combined and incongruities perceived by the intellect. When analysing humour, distinguish whether enjoyment is cognitive (surprise, mental connection) or affective (malice, triumph). This affects normative judgements about the morality of laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: 18th-century terminology: 'wit' vs 'humour' (classification of comic phenomena)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the eighteenth century 'wit' referred to clever verbal sayings, whereas 'humour' denoted a laughable character or temperament; the general category was often called 'the ridiculous' or 'the ludicrous'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this historical classification when interpreting period texts or evaluating examples: what was called 'humour' then may correspond today to character-based comedy, while 'wit' maps to verbal cleverness. This affects how theorists apply incongruity accounts: incongruity theory originally described wit more than character-based humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective vs subjective incongruity (Akenside)
rubrics_metrics.description: Incongruous properties may either exist in the objects themselves or in the apprehension of the perceiver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging whether something is ludicrous, ask whether the incongruity is an external feature of the objects/situation or arises from the audience's perception or misapprehension. This distinction bears on whether humour is grounded in the world or in cognitive framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social/contextual appropriateness of laughter (gentlemanly wit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriate laughter should encourage conviviality without being raucous or lower-class; wit should be congenial but not indecorous, witty but not unseemly, serious but not overly earnest — a 'middle way' between buffoonery and moroseness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eighteenth-century theorists (Addison, Kames, Hutcheson, etc.) prescribe moderation and taste: 'amiable humour' is a moral matter. Use this when evaluating or prescribing humour in social settings (e.g., coffee-houses vs ale-houses): does the humour fit the classed norms and conversational aims of the setting? Anti-patterns: excessive aristocratic disdain or bawdy hedonism; failure to balance conviviality and decorum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sociability criterion: humour's practical role in conversational contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Coffee-houses and salons required new codes of manners; laughter needed to be of an appropriate sort that would encourage conviviality and polite discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess humour by how well it supports the social function of a setting (e.g., facilitates agreeable discussion of art, commerce, politics) rather than disrupting it. Example: the coffee-house audience sought pleasantries that relaxed conversation without devolving into coarse behaviour.
